turns.speaker: CON

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Mari says tough questioning prevents harm, but that assumes pressure produces useful facts. Why should we trust answers obtained through fear instead of careful, lawful questioning that can be tested?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If a suspect knows an attack is imminent, should investigators really avoid tough questioning simply because the answers might be uncomfortable or incomplete?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: But Alice, if every firm question is dismissed as pressure, a dangerous suspect gets room to stall. Safeguards can reject abuse while still demanding direct answers when time matters.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your weakest point is that safeguards can make harsh questioning safe. Rules on paper do not erase fear, and a process that rewards pressure still risks unreliable answers and mistreatment.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When a credible threat is developing and ordinary questioning has failed, tough interrogation is necessary, provided questioning remains supervised and focused on preventing immediate harm.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: You call supervision a safeguard, but your claim depends on officials judging pressure correctly in a crisis. That condition is precisely when fear and haste can overwhelm good judgment.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Tough interrogation is necessary whenever a serious threat must be assessed and ordinary cooperation cannot provide the needed answer. Public protection sometimes demands disciplined pressure, not endless patience.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Yes, serious threats must be assessed, but that does not prove tough interrogation is necessary. Investigators can use evidence, patient questioning, and containment without making coercion their central method.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that patient questioning can work in many cases. But when a threat is immediate and cooperation fails, refusing tough interrogation leaves potential victims unprotected.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The small exception you describe is doing all the work. In real crises, officials may label ordinary uncertainty immediate danger, turning an emergency claim into permission for abuse.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine a suspect who knows where a hidden weapon is and refuses every question while an attack approaches. Firm, supervised interrogation could locate it and save lives.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That example proves only that urgency matters, not that toughness works. A suspect under pressure might invent a location, sending responders away while the real danger remains undiscovered.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: If careful questioning has failed and people face immediate danger, what stronger lawful method would you use to obtain critical information in time?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I would use containment, evidence, skilled questioning, and urgent investigation rather than coercion. Your demand for toughness risks trading one possible danger for many certain harms.
